newsitem.title: UK: East European Eurobond boom seen set to continue.
newsitem.headline: East European Eurobond boom seen set to continue.

text.p: Central and eastern European borrowers have raised more than $6 billion in Eurobonds this year and that amount, already a record, could double by the year-end, bankers said on Wednesday.
"The focus has been on Eastern Europe this year," a London banker said.
"Sovereigns in particular favour this market as it enables them to extend their debt maturity at cheaper funding levels and access a broader investor base."
Investor confidence has improved amid expectations of higher credit ratings for such countries as Russia.
The region has a significant need for funds, while moves towards membership of the European Union and a general push towards reform has also lifted investor sentiment.
The volume of eastern European bonds jumped to $6.2 billion in the first six months from $1.1 billion a year earlier, according to Capital DATA Bondware.

"We could match that ($6.2 billion) in the second half of this year, although the European 'summer lull' and the Christmas period does take some volume out of the market," a Eurobond syndicate manager said.
Supply for the whole of 1996 was $3.7 billion.

The market really took off after Russia's first Eurobond was launched last November. The $1 billion benchmark issue paved the way for others and carved a niche in the mushrooming emerging market sector, dealers said.

Russia has raised $4.1 billion on international bond markets since last November. Moscow and St Petersburg have also tapped the market and this week SBS-Agro became the first Russian bank to issue a fixed-rate Eurobond.
Croatia, the Czech Republic, Lithuania, Moldova, Poland, Romania and Slovenia have all borrowed this year.
Belarus, Bulgaria, Kazakhstan, Latvia, Macedonia, Slovakia and the Ukraine, among others, are eyeing the market, as well as scores of cities, banks and companies.

Bond maturities are expected to lengthen in coming months and the size of deals could increase as investors are able to allocate more to particular issuers and borrowers become more confident, bankers said.

David Boren, emerging market analyst at Salomon Brothers in London, said the fact that the U.S. Federal Reserve did not raise interest rates recently should trigger a string of issues on international capital markets.
"I think that especially some of the higher-yielding lower-rated countries are going to be accessing the market (later this year)," he said.
Peter Schikaneder, director in global markets at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said issuance would be driven by two factors -- interest rate stability and investors' quest for higher yields.
The second half is also expected to bring more variety in terms of the structure of transactions.

"Some sovereigns who came to market might switch strategy in terms of structures," an emerging market specialist said. "We expect more (U.S. domestic) Yankee bonds and different currencies as borrowers aim to set yield curves."
A battle among investment banks to establish themselves in the new markets of Eastern Europe benefits borrowers, bankers said.
"Banks will do deals at ridiculous levels to win a mandate," a trader at a U.S. bank said.
CSFB, J.P. Morgan and SBC Warburg have each underwritten more than $1 billion in issues from the region this year.
Most Eastern European borrowers raise funds in the dollar, mark or yen sectors but the market for Eurobonds denominated in their local currencies has also boomed.
Bonds denominated in the Czech crown, Croatian kuna, Polish zloty and Slovak crown are expected to increase.
"I expect a resurgence of emerging market currency supply, especially in Czech crowns and Polish zlotys," ABN AMRO Hoare Govett syndicate manager Ronnie Rana said.
Activity was dampened by a recent run on the Czech crown, dealers said, although confidence might return.
There have been 42 deals this year in Czech crowns, six in Polish zlotys, five in Slovak crowns and none in Croatian kuna, according to Capital DATA Bondware showed.
